chapters.title: Chapter 3: What Your ESOPs Are Really Worth

lessons.title: Valuing Your Options Simply: Fair Market Value, Intrinsic Value and Dilution

children.text: Ask an employee what their ESOPs are worth and you usually get one of two answers: a number from a WhatsApp forward about the last funding round, or a shrug. Both are wrong in the same way. They skip the three things that actually decide the answer: what you must pay, what sits ahead of you in the queue, and what still has to go right.

body.text: Your options are not worth your number of options times the last round price. They are worth what is left after the exercise price, after investor preferences, and after the probability that none of it happens.

children.text: Start With Intrinsic Value
Intrinsic value
is the simplest honest number: what your vested options would be worth if you exercised and sold today.

markDefs.definition: The value an option has if exercised today: fair market value minus exercise price, times the number of options. It cannot be less than zero.

body.caption: If fair market value sits below the exercise price, the options are said to be underwater and the intrinsic value is zero.

children.text: Priya holds 6,000 options at an exercise price of ₹50 in a company with 12,00,000 fully diluted shares valued at ₹200 each, so
fair market value
puts the company at ₹24 crore. Her intrinsic value is ₹9 lakh, and her stake is 0.5% fully diluted.

markDefs.definition: Fair Market Value: the value of one share on a given date, from the exchange for listed shares and from a registered valuer for unlisted ones.

body.text: Intrinsic value ignores time value: the worth of having years left before expiry while the share price can still move. Companies must value that properly for their accounts, usually with Black-Scholes under Ind AS 102, but for your own planning, intrinsic value plus a clear head about risk beats a model you cannot audit.

children.text: Dilution: Your Slice Shrinks, Your Money Need Not
Every new funding round issues new shares, so your percentage falls. That is
dilution
, and employees panic about it far more than they should.

markDefs.definition: The fall in your percentage ownership when a company issues new shares. It reduces your share of the pie, not necessarily the size of your slice in rupees.

children.text: Priya’s company raises ₹12 crore at ₹400 a share, issuing 3,00,000 new shares.

body.caption: One funding round, seen from Priya’s grant

children.text: Her ownership fell by 20%, from 0.5% to 0.4%. Her value rose by 133%, from ₹9 lakh to ₹21 lakh.
A smaller slice of a much larger pie is a good trade.
Dilution only hurts when the new shares are issued cheaply, as in a down round, or when they buy nothing useful.

body.title: Is Dilution Bad?
body.question: An employee holds 6,000 options at ₹50. The company raises at a higher price, and her fully diluted stake drops from 0.5% to 0.4%. What has happened to the value of her grant?
options: It has fallen by 20%, in line with her ownership
It is unchanged, since she still holds 6,000 options
It has risen, because the price per share more than doubled
It cannot be known without the exercise price
body.explanation: Her grant is a fixed number of options, not a fixed percentage. At ₹400 a share her intrinsic value is 6,000 × ₹350 = ₹21 lakh, against ₹9 lakh before. Percentage dilution and value are different questions, and the second one is the one that pays for things.

body.title: Value After the Round
body.prompt: After the round, the share price is ₹400. Priya holds 6,000 options at an exercise price of ₹50. What is the intrinsic value of her grant?
body.explanation: (₹400 minus ₹50) × 6,000 = ₹21,00,000. Her percentage fell while her value more than doubled.

children.text: The Queue Ahead of You: Liquidation Preference
This is the part almost nobody tells employees. Investors rarely buy ordinary shares. They buy preference shares carrying a
liquidation preference
, typically one times their money, paid out before ordinary shareholders and option holders see anything.

markDefs.definition: A right that pays certain investors a fixed amount out of exit proceeds before ordinary shareholders receive anything.

children.text: Suppose the company sells for ₹40 crore, below the ₹60 crore valuation of its last round. The investor put in ₹12 crore and holds 20% with a one times non-participating preference.

body.caption: Exit waterfall on a ₹40 crore sale

cells: Investor takes the higher of preference or pro rata
₹12 crore preference vs ₹8 crore pro rata
Left for ordinary shares and options

body.text: The naive calculation says 0.4% of ₹40 crore equals ₹16,00,000. The real answer is ₹11,00,000 after the preference and her exercise cost. In a soft exit, preferences can absorb most of the proceeds, and employees are last in the queue.

body.title: Why the last round price is not the value of your share

children.text: A preference share carries rights an ordinary share does not: a guaranteed first claim on exit proceeds, often anti-dilution protection, and sometimes a say over major decisions. Investors pay for those rights.

Your option converts into an ordinary share with none of them. So when a headline says a startup raised at a ₹4,000 crore valuation, that figure comes from applying the preference share price to every share, including yours. The merchant banker valuation used for your tax will often be lower, and rightly so.
It gets sharper in a
down round

, where new money comes in at a lower price and may carry a larger preference. Ordinary shareholders sit behind an even bigger queue. This is the main reason two employees with the same paper value can end up with wildly different outcomes.

markDefs.definition: A funding round priced below the previous round’s price per share.

body.title: Work the Waterfall
body.prompt: The company sells for ₹40 crore. The investor takes a ₹12 crore preference first. Priya’s 6,000 options represent 0.5% of the ordinary share base. Ignoring her exercise cost, what is her gross share of the proceeds?
body.explanation: ₹40 crore minus ₹12 crore leaves ₹28 crore for ordinary holders. 0.5% of that is ₹14,00,000. After paying ₹3,00,000 to exercise, she nets ₹11,00,000 before tax.

children.text: Finally, Weigh It by What Might Actually Happen
A single number pretends the future is certain. A short scenario table is more honest, and takes two minutes.

body.title: Priya’s net outcome across four futures

body.caption: Probability weighted value of the same grant

children.text: On these assumptions the grant is worth about ₹23.85 lakh in expectation, not the ₹21 lakh headline and certainly not the ₹16,00,000 the naive exit maths suggested. Change the probabilities to your own and the arithmetic still works. The discipline of writing the failure case down is the point.

stats.context: At the latest round price, ignoring everything else

body.title: Valuing Any Grant in Six Steps
steps: Get the number of options, the exercise price and the fully diluted share count.
Work out your percentage: options divided by fully diluted shares.
Compute intrinsic value: (fair market value minus exercise price) times options.
Ask how much capital investors have put in, and what liquidation preference it carries.
Subtract the preference from a realistic exit value before taking your percentage.
Weigh the result by an honest probability of success, and only then compare it with a cash salary.

body.title: Two Offers, One Spreadsheet
body.scenario: Karan has two offers. Company A, a listed mid-cap in Mumbai, offers ₹28 lakh cash and RSUs worth about ₹6 lakh a year at today’s market price. Company B, a Series B startup, offers ₹22 lakh cash and 20,000 options at a ₹60 exercise price, with the last round priced at ₹310 a share and about ₹180 crore raised across rounds carrying one times preferences.
body.prompt: How should Karan compare the two, and what should he ask Company B?
body.modelAnswer: He should convert both to comparable annual numbers and then discount the risky one. Company A is roughly ₹34 lakh a year, and the RSUs are liquid and lose value only if the share falls. Company B is ₹22 lakh cash plus options whose headline intrinsic value is 20,000 × ₹250 = ₹50 lakh, but that vests over four years, is illiquid, and sits behind ₹180 crore of preferences, so any exit below that figure leaves ordinary shareholders with nothing. A fair comparison is ₹12 lakh a year of headline option value, then discounted for the probability of a good exit and for the fact that he must fund ₹12 lakh of exercise cost plus perquisite tax at some point. Questions for Company B: what is the fully diluted share count, so he can convert 20,000 options into a percentage; how much has been raised and on what preference terms; what the latest merchant banker valuation says, as against the preference share price; how long the exercise window runs after leaving; and whether the company has ever run a buyback.

points: Intrinsic value is fair market value minus exercise price, times options, and never less than zero.
Dilution cuts your percentage, not necessarily your value. Priya went from 0.5% to 0.4% while her grant went from ₹9 lakh to ₹21 lakh.
Investors hold preference shares, so their money usually comes out of an exit before yours.
In the soft exit here, the naive answer was ₹16,00,000 and the real one was ₹11,00,000 after preference and exercise cost.
The last round price values preference shares, not the ordinary shares your options convert into.
Weigh outcomes by probability, and write down the case where the company fails.
Always ask for the fully diluted share count, the capital raised and the preference terms. Without those three, any valuation of your grant is guesswork.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. All companies, probabilities and figures here are illustrative, and the probabilities in particular are assumptions chosen to show the method, not estimates for any real company.
